content: Five physicians were trained in the Nutrition and Care for Development modules, while six physicians served as controls. For each physician, a trained anthropologist conducted structured observations of five clinical consultations involving children under two years of age. Caregivers of these children were interviewed shortly after the consultations to assess their recall and understanding of the counseling provided. Approximately half of the 109 caregiver-child pairs were in the intervention group. One group of 68 caregiver-child pairs was observed during the physician session, interviewed at the exit, and followed up one week later. The other group of 41 pairs was not observed but was interviewed at the exit only. Caregivers' memory of the counseling messages and their intention to perform the recommended activities were evaluated. Results showed that all but one of the five intervention physicians made recommendations for Care for Development. However, communication-related recommendations (79%) were more frequently provided than play-related recommendations (60%). Intervention physicians were significantly more likely to praise the mother (70% vs. 19%) and check her understanding (78% vs. 32%) compared to controls. When the Care for Development module was used, the average session time increased from 20 to 27 minutes. All observed mothers recalled some of the counseling messages during both the exit interview and the follow-up interview seven days later. The most commonly recalled messages included: initiating conversations with sounds or gestures, providing safe household items for the child to handle, offering large colorful objects for the child to reach for, playing with the child, and responding to the child's sounds. Although physicians were less likely to provide play-related messages than communication-related ones, four of the five most frequently recalled messages were about play. Mothers who were interviewed but not observed also remembered at least one message and recalled the same set of items. Among the intervention group, approximately 66% of mothers were already engaging in the recommended activities, while the remainder reported attempting them. The field test demonstrated that physicians can be trained to assess developmental needs, provide recommendations, and that mothers can recall and implement these recommendations. In southern Brazil, many of these activities were already being practiced. Physicians suggested that the Care for Development training should include more exercises, as they felt less confident about developmental levels and more comfortable with communication items than play items. They also recommended the inclusion of a training video. In South Africa, a field test evaluated the implementation of an improved Care for Development training model for nurses within the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) framework. A before-and-after design was used, with structured observations of consultations and exit interviews with caregivers. In the Western Cape, 21 nurses were trained in Care for Development and Feeding. A subgroup was observed a week before the training, and all 21 nurses were observed during the training. Trained nurses showed significant improvements in responsiveness to caregivers, with praise increasing from 10% during the pretest to 58% during training and 72% a week later. Checking caregivers' understanding increased from 7% pretest to 58% during training and 67% later. Encouraging caregivers to talk increased from 38% pretest to 64% during training. The authors concluded that the modified IMCI training was highly effective in improving health workers' communication and counseling performance in the short term. However, they acknowledged that the pretest/post-test design, with supervisors observing nurses during sessions, might reduce the study's validity. Despite this limitation, the observed behavior changes were substantial. The authors noted that nurses who practiced feeding and Care for Development separately performed better than those who combined the two, though no explanation was provided. They also commented on the relatively poor recall and responses of caregivers, particularly regarding play and communication during exit interviews, but no data were presented. In Turkey, the first efficacy evaluation of the Care for Development module was conducted in 2004 at the University of Ankara's Department of Pediatrics. The hypothesis was that the intervention group would engage in more play and communication activities at home one month after the intervention compared to the control group, as measured by the Home Observation Measurement of the Environment (HOME) Scale. Two physicians initially saw 113 children for illness in the hospital and then at home one month later. After receiving training, the physicians saw 120 caregiver-child pairs, most of whom returned for a follow-up visit seven days later. They were also observed in their homes using the HOME Scale one month later. The sample was recruited from the Ankara Pediatric Outpatient Clinic, serving lowto middle-income families. Only children aged 24 months or younger with minor illnesses or those attending well-baby care were included. There were no differences between groups in socioeconomic status or illness measures. The intervention group showed significantly higher scores on the HOME Scale compared to the control group. At the one-week follow-up, 88% of children had recovered, and the intervention group had significantly fewer incorrect medications. Patient satisfaction was high in both groups. The authors concluded that the Care for Development intervention effectively supports caregivers in providing a more stimulating environment for their children and can be integrated into visits for minor illnesses. However, the long-term impact of such brief interventions remains to be investigated. In rural China, a second efficacy trial evaluated the Care for Development intervention using child development measures as outcomes. The study involved 100 children under two years of age, randomly assigned to intervention and control groups. Mothers received two face-to-face guidance sessions on good childcare practices based on WHO guidelines, delivered at the beginning of the six-month period and two months later. Local village doctors were also trained using videos, reading materials, and problem-solving exercises. At six months, child development was assessed using the Gesell Development Scale, and mothers' knowledge and understanding of the recommendations were evaluated through a questionnaire. Doctors' knowledge and confidence in managing young children's health were assessed before and after training. Mothers in the intervention group showed significant improvements in knowledge and skills related to early childcare. Doctors demonstrated increased ability to practice the learned skills. Children in the intervention group scored significantly higher in fine motor, speech, and interpersonal communication skills compared to the control group, particularly in adaptive skills, language development, and cognitive development. However, no differences were observed in motor scores. A limitation of the study was that the same person who tested the children also conducted the intervention. In Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, studies assessed the implementation of the intervention in a random sample of families in intervention districts. Child development was evaluated using the Tajik Early Learning and Development Standards and the Ages and Stages Questionnaire. Health workers who received training were significantly more likely to ask about and make recommendations for Care for Development. Caregivers in intervention areas were more likely to recall Care for Development messages and report engaging in new activities with their children. Families in intervention areas were also more likely to have seen Care for Development materials, though the differences were not large. Overall, these studies suggest that interventions to provide recommendations and problem-solving support to parents through public health systems can effectively improve family stimulation behaviors and young children's development. The time and investment required for implementation are relatively small, with interventions adding approximately 5-10 minutes per visit. Ongoing studies in Pakistan, India, and Australia are investigating the long-term impacts of Care for Development materials, local adaptations, and integration within existing services for children under three years of age. Preliminary data from Pakistan indicate promising results, with families and health workers accepting the intervention and early benefits observed in growth and development.
